title: Family and people
objectives: Name family members and use Ate, Kuya, Tito, Tita naturally
Use the topic marker ang, and si/sina before names
Point people and things out with ito, iyan, iyon
Say what you have and don't have with may, mayroon, and wala

grammar.title: The marker ang — and si/sina for names
grammar.explanation:
Tagalog nouns almost never stand alone; a small marker in front tells you their job in the sentence. The first marker to learn is ang. It marks the topic — the person or thing the sentence is about. (Grammars call words in this role the 'ang-form'; we'll call it the topic or doer form.) Guro ang lalaki — 'The man is a teacher': the description guro comes first, then ang points at who we're talking about.

Names of people take si instead of ang: Guro si Ben — 'Ben is a teacher.' For two or more named people, use sina: Estudyante sina Ana at Liza — 'Ana and Liza are students.'

You already know the pronouns ako, ka, siya and friends — they are the pronoun versions of ang-marked words, which is why the patterns match: Guro siya. Guro si Ben. Guro ang lalaki.

One more small tool: to say 'my', put ko after the noun — ang nanay ko, 'my mom'. The full set of these possessive words comes in the next unit; for now just use ko.

examples.tl: Kaklase ko sina Liza at Carlos.
examples.en: Liza and Carlos are my classmates.

grammar.title: Pointing things out: ito, iyan, iyon
grammar.explanation:
Tagalog has three pointing words where English has two. Ito = 'this' (near me, the speaker). Iyan = 'that' (near you, the listener). Iyon = 'that over there' (far from both of us).

To introduce someone, point with ito plus si: Ito si Ana, ang kapatid ko — 'This is Ana, my sister.' To ask who someone is: Sino ito? / Sino iyan? — 'Who is this/that?' For things: Ano iyan? — 'What is that (you're holding)?'

The pattern is the same as with pronouns — description first, pointer second, no word for 'is': Nanay ko ito ('This is my mom'), or pointer first when introducing: Ito ang bahay namin is for later; at this stage, stick to Ito si... for people and Ito ang... for things.

examples.tl: Ano ito? — Litrato ito ng pamilya ko.
examples.en: What is this? — This is a photo of my family.

grammar.title: Having and not having: may, mayroon, wala
grammar.explanation:
May means 'have' or 'there is/are'. It goes directly before a bare noun: May kapatid ako — 'I have a sibling.' May aso sila — 'They have a dog.' Notice there's no marker on the noun after may.

Mayroon (often shortened to meron in speech) means the same thing but stands on its own or takes little words after it. Use it to answer yes: May kapatid ka ba? — Mayroon. ('Do you have siblings? — I do.') With po: Mayroon po.

Wala is the opposite: 'none / don't have / there isn't'. Wala akong kapatid — 'I have no siblings.' As a bare answer: Wala po. Notice wala takes -ng before its noun (walang) — that's the linker you'll formally meet in Unit 5; for now memorize walang + noun and mayroong + noun as chunks.

Common beginner mistake: using hindi to answer May...? questions. 'Do you have a dog?' — the answer is Wala (none), never Hindi.

examples.tl: May aso ba kayo? — Mayroon po.
examples.en: Do you have a dog? — We do.
I don't have any cousins here.

vocab.note: Also ina (formal); mama is common too
Also ama (formal); papa is common too
Also used to address any slightly older woman politely

example.en: This is my older sister Liza.

vocab.note: Also used to address any slightly older man politely

example.en: My older brother is still a student.
That over there is Grandpa Ben.

example.tl: Sino ang lalaki? — Kuya ko iyan.
example.en: Who is the man? — That's my older brother.
They have a house in Cebu.
This is a photo of my family.

vocab.en: marker before two or more names

example.tl: Kaibigan ko sina Ana at Ben.
example.en: Ana and Ben are my friends.
That over there is our house.

vocab.note: Shortened to meron in casual speech

example.tl: May kapatid ka ba? — Mayroon po.
example.en: Do you have siblings? — Yes, I do.

vocab.note: Takes the linker before a noun: walang aso
Pairs with na (already): bata pa = still young

dialogue.title: A family photo
dialogue.context: Ben shows Kate a photo of his family on his phone.

lines.speaker: Ben
lines.tl: Kate, ito ang litrato ng pamilya ko.
lines.en: Kate, this is a photo of my family.

lines.speaker: Kate
lines.tl: Ay, malaki ang pamilya mo! Sino ito?
lines.en: Oh, your family is big! Who is this?

lines.speaker: Ben
lines.tl: Ito si Nanay, at ito naman si Tatay.
lines.en: This is Mom, and this here is Dad.

lines.speaker: Kate
lines.en: Who is that? Is that your sibling?

lines.speaker: Ben
lines.tl: Oo, ito si Ate Liza. Guro siya.
lines.en: Yes, this is my older sister Liza. She's a teacher.

lines.speaker: Ben
lines.tl: Anak ni Ate Liza. Limang taon na siya.
lines.en: That's Ate Liza's child. He's five years old.

lines.speaker: Kate
lines.tl: Ang cute! May kapatid ka pa ba?
lines.en: So cute! Do you have other siblings?

lines.speaker: Ben
lines.tl: Mayroon. Ito si Kuya Carlos. Ikaw, may kapatid ka ba?
lines.en: I do. This is my older brother Carlos. How about you, do you have siblings?

lines.speaker: Kate
lines.tl: Wala akong kapatid. Pero may aso kami!
lines.en: I don't have siblings. But we have a dog!

lines.speaker: Ben
lines.tl: Talaga? Kami rin! Ito ang aso namin, si Bantay.
lines.en: Really? Us too! This is our dog, Bantay.

exercises.prompt: Which marker goes before a single person's name?
exercises.explain: Names take si (Estudyante si Ana); ang is for ordinary nouns and sina is for two or more names.
Ate is your older sister — and Filipinos also use it to politely address any slightly older woman.

exercises.prompt: ___ si Ana at ito naman si Ben. (Introducing two people one by one: 'This is Ana...')
exercises.explain: Ito ('this, near me') plus si introduces a person: Ito si Ana.

exercises.prompt: Your friend is holding a photo. You ask 'Who is that (in your hand)?' Which pointer is right?
exercises.explain: Iyan points at something near the listener; ito is near you, and iyon is far from both of you.

exercises.prompt: Estudyante ___ Ana at Liza. (Ana and Liza are students.)
exercises.explain: Two or more names take the plural marker sina instead of si.

exercises.tl: May dalawang kapatid ako at isang aso.
exercises.explain: May dalawang kapatid = 'I have two siblings', and isang aso = 'one dog'.

exercises.prompt: May pusa ka ba? You have no cat. Which is the correct answer?
exercises.explain: Questions with may are answered with mayroon (have) or wala (none) — never with hindi.

exercises.prompt: ___ akong kapatid, pero may pinsan ako. (I have no siblings, but I have a cousin.)
exercises.explain: Wala + -ng expresses not having: Wala akong kapatid = 'I don't have siblings'.

exercises.prompt: This is my mom. She is a teacher.
exercises.answer: Ito ang nanay ko. Guro siya.
accept: Ito ang nanay ko. Guro siya
Ito po ang nanay ko. Guro po siya
exercises.explain: Ito introduces her, ang nanay ko is 'my mom' (ko = my), and Guro siya needs no word for 'is'.

exercises.tl: Sino iyon? — Iyon si Lolo. Matanda na siya.
exercises.explain: Iyon points at someone far from both speakers, and lolo is grandfather.

exercises.prompt: May tatlong anak sina Tito Ramon at Tita Rosa.
exercises.answer: Uncle Ramon and Aunt Rosa have three children.
accept: Uncle Ramon and Aunt Rosa have three children
Tito Ramon and Tita Rosa have three children
Uncle Ramon and Auntie Rosa have three kids
exercises.explain: May tatlong anak = 'have three children'; sina marks the named couple as the ones who have them.

exercises.prompt: Do you have a dog? — We don't. But we have two cats.
exercises.answer: May aso ba kayo? — Wala. Pero may dalawang pusa kami.
accept: May aso ba kayo? Wala. Pero may dalawang pusa kami
May aso ba kayo? Wala po. Pero may dalawang pusa kami
May aso ka ba? Wala. Pero may dalawang pusa kami
May aso ba kayo? Wala. May dalawang pusa kami
exercises.explain: May + noun asks about having; the negative answer is wala, and may dalawang pusa kami states what you do have.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence says 'The woman is my neighbor'?
exercises.explain: Description first (kapitbahay ko, 'my neighbor'), then ang babae marks who the sentence is about. Babae is an ordinary noun, so it takes ang, not si.
